title: What are default and static methods in interfaces, and why were default methods added for backward compatibility (e.g. `forEach` on Collections)?
shortTitle: What are default and static methods in interfaces?
keyPoints: Default methods have a body in the interface and are inherited by all implementing classes without requiring an override.
Static methods belong to the interface namespace, called via InterfaceName.method(), and are NOT inherited.
The primary motivation was backward compatibility: adding forEach, stream, and removeIf to Iterable and Collection without breaking implementations.
Implementing classes can override default methods to provide custom behaviour while inheriting others for free.
Default methods enable interface evolution: adding new functionality to published APIs without breaking existing code.
Static methods replace companion utility classes: Comparator.comparing() instead of ComparatorUtils.comparing().
Default methods participate in polymorphism: calling a default method on a subclass dispatches to the override if one exists.

s1_definition.oneliner: Default methods have a body in the interface and enable backward-compatible API evolution; static methods are interface-scoped utilities called via InterfaceName.method() and are not inherited.
s1_definition.profdef:
- **Default method** has the `default` keyword and a method body. Implementing classes inherit it without overriding but can override if needed.
- **Static method** belongs to the interface itself. Called only via `InterfaceName.method()`. Not inherited by implementing classes.
- **Backward compatibility** was the primary motivation: Java 8 needed to add `forEach()`, `stream()`, `removeIf()`, and `sort()` to existing interfaces without breaking millions of implementations.
- **Interface evolution** means published APIs can add new methods without requiring every implementor to update their code.
- **Polymorphism** works with default methods: if an implementing class overrides a default, the overridden version is called.
- **Key additions in Java 8**: `Iterable.forEach`, `Collection.stream`, `Collection.removeIf`, `List.sort`, `Map.getOrDefault`, `Map.computeIfAbsent`.
s1_definition.analogy: Imagine the RBI (Reserve Bank of India) mandates that all banks must add UPI transfer as a service. Before Java 8, every bank (implementing class) had to write the UPI logic individually: 100 banks, 100 implementations, some might miss it. With default methods, the RBI provides a default UPI implementation in the banking interface itself. Banks get it automatically. If HDFC wants a custom implementation, it overrides. If SBI is fine with the default, it does nothing. Zero breaking changes.

sections.s6_takeaway:
Default methods were added in Java 8 primarily for backward compatibility. The Java team needed to add methods like forEach, stream, and removeIf to existing interfaces, but adding abstract methods would break millions of implementing classes worldwide. Default methods provide a method body directly in the interface, so implementing classes inherit the behaviour automatically without any code change. ArrayList got forEach, stream, and sort without modifying its source code.

Static methods on interfaces are utility methods that belong to the interface namespace, called via InterfaceName.method(). Unlike default methods, they are not inherited and cannot be overridden. They replace the old companion utility class pattern: Comparator.comparing() instead of a separate ComparatorUtils class.

In Rajesh's account service at National Bank of India, the AccountService interface has one abstract method (getBalance) and two default methods (getFormattedBalance and isOverdrawn). SavingsAccountService only implements getBalance and gets both defaults for free. CurrentAccountService overrides getFormattedBalance with custom formatting but inherits isOverdrawn.

Remember one sentence: default methods let interfaces evolve without breaking implementations, and static methods replace companion utility classes.
